\viewkind4\uc1\pard\f0\fs24 Agreement approved, as amended, in the total not-to-exceed amount of $500,000.00 per fiscal year, including $100,000.00 for program administration and $400,000.00 for competitive grant awards and event production. Funds for administrative services will be prepaid. Visit St. Pete-Clearwater President and CEO Brian Lowack is authorized to distribute the remainder of the funding upon approval of the programs proposed by Creative Pinellas. Agreement will be effective upon execution by the Board of County Commissioners through December 31, 2026, with automatic one-year renewal terms, unless terminated, in accordance with the agreement. \par
\par
Commissioner Peters made a motion for approval, which was seconded by Commissioner Scott; whereupon, Commissioner Scherer expressed concern regarding awarding the full agreement amount of $500,000.00 without knowing how Creative Pinellas will utilize the funds. \par
\par
At Mr. Burton\rquote s request, Mr. Lowack provided information regarding clawback provisions incorporated into the agreement by the County Attorney\rquote s Office; whereupon, discussion ensued wherein Mr. Lowack and Creative Pinellas Chief Executive Officer Margaret Murray, with input from Mr. Burton, responded to comments and queries by the members and discussed the proposed agreement, including details related to the process for awarding funds to artists and the funding timeline. During discussion, Commissioners Peters and Scott indicated that they would accept a friendly amendment to the motion.\par
\par
Commissioner Scherer indicated that he would propose an amendment to the motion, which would stipulate that the Board prepay $100,000.00 for project administration and authorize Mr. Lowack to distribute the remainder of the funding upon approval of the programs put forward by Creative Pinellas.\tab\par
\par
Further discussion ensued, with input from Ms. Murray and Mr. Lowack, regarding the distribution of grant funds and the terms of the amendment; whereupon, Commissioner Peters seconded the amendment.\par
\par
Responding to a query by Commissioner Peters, Attorney White advised that the Board retain language related to clawback provisions in the proposed agreement and grant authority to the County Administrator and County Attorney to finalize the contract language.\cf1\f1\fs22\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\f0\fs24 Mr. Burton indicated that he requested that Community Development Planning Division Manager Bruce Bussey provide an update regarding the Penny IV Affordable Housing Program. He related that, based on the amount of funds spent and the number of applications submitted, staff is recommending that no new Penny IV applications be accepted at this time; and that, with the Board\rquote s approval, staff will then evaluate the previously submitted applications and make recommendations to commit the balance of the available funds.\par
\par
Referring to a document titled \i Penny IV Affordable Housing Program\i0 , Mr. Bussey provided information regarding the program, including that, since the program launched in 2020, $91.2 million has been committed to 18 multifamily affordable housing development projects; and that, once completed, the projects will have produced 3,164 new housing units, of which 2,227 will be restricted affordable units for various income levels; whereupon, he explained that the ten-year set-aside for the program recently decreased from $99.8 million to $94.1 million, which leaves approximately $2.9 million in uncommitted funds; and that staff is currently working on two project recommendations, which would fully commit the remaining funds.\par
\par
Mr. Bussey also highlighted additional program metrics related to the amount of funds leveraged by the program and the average subsidy per unit; whereupon, in response to a query by Chair Eggers, he indicated that while staff does not currently have data pertaining to potential tax revenues generated by the affordable housing development projects funded through the program, staff can conduct research to collect the information. Responding to comments and queries by Commissioner Peters, Messrs. Bussey and Burton also provided brief comments related to a recently resolved technical issue, which affected a potential applicant, and staff\rquote s plans to inform potential applicants of the program\rquote s change in status.\par
\par
Following brief discussion, Chair Eggers confirmed that there is consensus to discontinue acceptance of Penny IV applications beginning tomorrow, March 25; whereupon, in response to comments by Chair Eggers, Mr. Bussey noted that staff will continue to work with applicants by utilizing alternative funding sources.\par
\par
Thereupon, Mr. Burton provided brief comments related to the Board\rquote s upcoming Work Session, which is scheduled for April 2, and noted that the agenda includes a lengthy presentation regarding surface water management.\cf1\f1\fs22\par
}

{\rtf1\ansi\ansicpg1252\deff0\deflang1033{\fonttbl{\f0\fswiss\fprq2\fcharset0 Arial;}{\f1\froman\fprq2\fcharset2 Symbol;}{\f2\fnil\fcharset0 Arial;}}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\f0\fs24 Resolution No. 26-25 adopted, declaring multiple County-owned properties in downtown Clearwater as surplus and granting authorization to the County Administrator to advertise the properties for sale through a competitive request for negotiations (RFN) process.\par
\par
Mr. Burton introduced the item and, upon the Chair\rquote s request, explained that the proposed action is to declare multiple properties owned by the County and located within the City of Clearwater as surplus; that a negotiation process to execute the sale of the subject properties is still required; and that staff will issue an RFN on a later date, at which time the members may review proposals for use of the properties.\par
\par
Chair Eggers indicated that residents will be given an opportunity to provide public comment regarding the sale of the properties at a town hall meeting scheduled for April 23; and that public notice for the meeting will soon be published.\par
\par
Responding to queries by Commissioner Scherer and Chair Eggers, Mr. Burton, with input from Assistant County Administrator Blaine Williams, discussed various topics related to the RFN, including the following:\par
\par
\pard\fi-360\li360\f1\'b7\tab\f0 Approval process\par
\f1\'b7\tab\f0 Status of the draft RFN and its various components\par
\f1\'b7\tab\f0 Distribution of the draft to the members\par
\f1\'b7\tab\f0 Timeline of release\par
\f1\'b7\tab\f0 Role of citizen input\par
\pard\par
In response to an additional query by Chair Eggers, Mr. Burton confirmed that a review of the RFN can be added to the agenda of the Board\rquote s April 30 work session; whereupon, responding to a query by Commissioner Latvala, Mr. Williams indicated that, as the real estate broker for the project, CBRE will receive a commission from the sale of the subject properties. In response to queries by Commissioners Latvala and Nowicki, Mr. Burton provided details regarding the process associated with selecting CBRE for this project and their work related to other projects throughout the county.\par
\par
Responding to comments by Commissioner Nowicki, Mr. Burton explained that CBRE did not prepare a financial analysis comparing the sale of the properties to a ground lease due to the number of variables and assumptions involved, which make it difficult to provide an accurate side-by-side comparison; whereupon, discussion ensued regarding sale versus ground lease options, timing of the Board\rquote s action in relation to planned community input, and flexibility within the RFN process.\par
\par
In response to a query by Commissioner Peters, Attorney White indicated that she believes there was a consensus during a previous work session to proceed with CBRE\rquote s recommendation; whereupon, she clarified that declaring the County-owned properties as surplus is a preliminary step prior to issuance of the RFN and does not obligate the Board to proceed with either option; and that all options will remain available, regardless of the Board\rquote s action today.\par
\par
Responding to queries by Chair Eggers, Mr. Burton clarified that this item was previously on the March 24 meeting agenda; and that it was postponed to today\rquote s meeting to allow a work session and discussion with CBRE to take place.\par
\par

{\rtf1\ansi\ansicpg1252\deff0\deflang1033{\fonttbl{\f0\fswiss\fprq2\fcharset0 Arial;}{\f1\froman\fprq2\fcharset2 Symbol;}{\f2\fnil\fcharset0 Arial;}}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\f0\fs24 Resolution No. 26-30 adopted, amending the Clearwater-Largo Road Community Redevelopment District Plan, as outlined in the Staff Report. Proposal to create a 20-year term redevelopment Trust Fund and to establish the County\rquote s Tax Increment Financing (TIF) contribution rates, denied. Staff directed to work with the City of Largo to draft an interlocal agreement containing a County contribution of less than 50%, which will be brought back to the Board for approval. No correspondence has been received.\par
\par
Referring to a PowerPoint presentation, Housing and Community Development Strategic Initiatives Manager Rebecca Stonefield provided background information regarding the Clearwater-Largo Road Community Redevelopment Area (CLR-CRA). She related that the CRA was established in the mid-1990s and has undergone several boundary expansions, the most recent of which was approved by the Board in 2023; and that no Trust Fund or TIF mechanism has been established for the CRA to date.\par
\par
Ms. Stonefield explained that the Board is now being asked to approve an update to the CRA's redevelopment plan in order to address the 2023 expansion area and to approve an ordinance which would establish a 20-year redevelopment Trust Fund; whereupon, she noted that the CRA's redevelopment plan update is intended to ensure consistency with the Countywide Plan and the Advantage Alt 19 plan; and that the update would also support mixed-use development, walkable neighborhoods, transit-oriented design, and catalytic projects that could improve blight conditions within the CRA.\par
\par
Ms. Stonefield described the location and boundaries of the CLR-CRA and reviewed the County\rquote s scoring methodology for determining the level of TIF contribution for which a CRA qualifies. She indicated that the CLR-CRA qualifies for the Urban Revitalization designation, which aligns with a maximum total contribution of 95%; and that the City of Largo is requesting a 75% County contribution, which includes a priority match that is contingent on a minimum of 50% of the annual CRA budget being directed toward County priority areas, such as affordable housing and economic development; whereupon, Ms. Stonefield noted that, based on a projected 4% annual taxable value growth rate, the County\rquote s TIF contribution is estimated at approximately $5.3 million over 10 years and $23.2 million over 20 years.\par
\par
Thereupon, Ms. Stonefield outlined the Board\rquote s options with regard to the Trust Fund ordinance, noting that, per State statute, approval would require a minimum County TIF contribution of 50%; and that, if the members wished to consider a lower contribution, the Board could deny the ordinance and direct staff to negotiate an interlocal agreement. She also noted that the ordinance includes a ten-year midpoint review, at which time the City would report on progress made and the use of TIF funds; and that the Board would then have the opportunity to reassess the level of County TIF contribution.\par
\par
Attorney Crowell clarified that this item is legislative in nature, not quasi-judicial; whereupon, City of Largo Assistant Community Development Director Christopher Tillett provided an overview of the City\rquote s vision for the CLR-CRA, noting that its goals are to preserve the character of existing single-family residential neighborhoods, incentivize increased density and intensity along U.S. Alternate 19 and Clearwater-Largo Road, and improve connectivity within the CRA.\line\line Mr. Tillett reviewed the CRA\rquote s current economic challenges, including that the median household income, unemployment rate, vehicle access, and crime rate all reflect significant deficiencies when compared to City and County averages. He also indicated that the City has historically relied on competitive grant funding sources, which are limited and project-specific, making long-term planning difficult; and that the CRA has experienced significant economic lag, as demonstrated by lower property values and aging building stock in commercial areas; whereupon, Mr. Tillett noted that the City is committed to directing over 70% of both City and County funds toward County core priorities, including stormwater infrastructure, pedestrian connectivity, and infill housing development.\par
\par
Additionally, Mr. Tillett emphasized the importance of County TIF contributions and related that a City-only TIF would generate limited revenue and delay meaningful infrastructure improvements. He also noted that the CRA\rquote s current taxable value is approximately $611,600,000.00, generating approximately $2.8 million each year in County tax revenue; and that, at the projected end of the TIF term, the CRA\rquote s taxable value is estimated to reach approximately $1.3 billion, which would generate approximately $6.2 million in County tax revenue each year and represent an estimated 120% return on the County\rquote s investment.\par
\par
In response to comments and queries by Chair Eggers and Commissioner Flowers, Ms. Stonefield and Mr. Tillett provided clarifying information regarding the proposed County TIF contribution structure and the inclusion of both the original and expanded CRA areas within the proposed term and TIF calculation; whereupon, Commissioner Scott indicated that while he supports the CRA's redevelopment plan, he has concerns regarding the use of countywide taxpayer funds for CRA contributions. Commissioner Scott then made a motion to approve the CRA's redevelopment plan amendment, noting that consideration of any County TIF contribution should be addressed separately.\par
\par
Responding to comments and queries by the members, Ms. Stonefield and Mr. Tillett, with input from Mr. Burton and City of Largo City Manager John Curp, discussed various topics, including the following:\par
\par
\pard\fi-360\li360\f1\'b7\tab\f0 County\rquote s existing and potential CRA funding obligations\par
\f1\'b7\tab\f0 Structure and level of the proposed County TIF contribution\par
\f1\'b7\tab\f0 Alternative approaches to funding, including the use of an interlocal agreement\par
\pard\li360\par
\pard Commissioner Nowicki then made a motion to deny the Trust Fund and direct coordination of an interlocal agreement with no County contribution. The motion was seconded by Commissioner Scott; whereupon, in response to the Chair\rquote s call for public comment, City of Largo Mayor Woody Brown, Largo, appeared and provided brief comments.\par
\par
Discussion ensued regarding Commissioner Nowicki\rquote s motion and whether the County\rquote s TIF contribution should be reduced to zero or just below the minimum threshold of 50% which is required to establish a Trust Fund; whereupon, Commissioner Nowicki amended his motion to deny the Trust Fund and instruct staff to work with the City of Largo to develop an interlocal agreement containing a County contribution of less than 50%, which will be brought back to the Board for approval. The motion was seconded by Commissioner Scott.\par
\par
Following brief clarification by Attorney Crowell regarding the need for two votes by the Board, Commissioner Flowers seconded Commissioner Scott\rquote s earlier motion to approve the CRA's redevelopment plan.\cf1\f2\fs22\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\ul\f0\fs24 Direction on Downtown Redevelopment\par
\ulnone\par
Mr. Burton indicated that staff has prepared a request for negotiation (RFN) for the redevelopment and revitalization of downtown Clearwater and the County\rquote s downtown Clearwater campus; that CBRE Group, Inc. Executive Vice President Lee Ann Korst will be providing a brief presentation as part of staff\rquote s request for the Board\rquote s approval to move forward with the RFN; and that Chief Assistant County Attorney Don Crowell will introduce the legal counsel for the RFN. He also related that the RFN will likely be released in June and does not specify a preference for either a lease or fee simple ownership structure.\par
\par
Ms. Korst explained that members of CBRE Group, Inc. have developed a process through which developers may submit proposals utilizing their preferred transaction structure of either a ground lease or fee simple ownership model, along with associated legal protections and controls; that qualified developers will be brought back to the Board for presentations; and that a Town Hall meeting will then be held prior to the Board making a decision.\par
\par
Attorney Crowell introduced outside counsel Eric Singer, who is with the Bilzin Sumberg law firm, and indicated that Mr. Singer has been hired to assist the County with this project; and that he has previously represented both local governments and developers; whereupon, Mr. Singer provided brief comments regarding previous discussions with the County Attorney\rquote s Office related to obtaining market feedback associated with the RFN process and transaction structures. \par
\par
Responding to a query by Commissioner Flowers, Ms. Korst confirmed that developers may submit proposals utilizing a combination of transaction structures for different noncontiguous properties within the redevelopment area.\par
\par
In response to comments and queries by Commissioner Latvala, Attorney Crowell discussed factors associated with the RFN process and applicant proposals, including developer experience, financial capacity, proposed uses, and project activation timelines. Mr. Burton then indicated that the County would not be obligated to accept any proposals that do not align with its objectives; whereupon, Attorney Crowell also noted that the RFN will contain considerations that are completely separated from any religious affiliation of a developer. \par
\par
Brief discussion ensued regarding redevelopment considerations and long-term control of downtown Clearwater properties; whereupon, in response to comments and queries by the members, Ms. Korst and Mr. Singer discussed various transaction and development options, including partial ownership of a structure through the construction of upper-level condominiums, a 99-year ground lease, and fee simple ownership. \par
\par
In response to a query by Chair Eggers, Ms. Korst explained that developers will be asked to provide feedback regarding an extensive list of indicative terms compiled by Mr. Singer; whereupon, brief discussion ensued regarding community concerns related to long-term ownership and redevelopment of the downtown Clearwater properties.\par
\par
Responding to comments by Chair Eggers, Mr. Burton clarified that while staff would like to identify one master developer, he expects to see a combination of uses throughout the development area; that public input regarding any proposed structures will be received before the Board makes a final decision; that staff decided to release an RFN rather than to immediately proceed under a fee simple structure due to feedback received from the Board and the public; and that Mr. Singer was hired to provide legal assistance with the indicative terms; whereupon, Mr. Singer provided brief comments regarding the development of ground lease and fee simple development structures and the ability for the County to receive fair value under either model.\par
\par
In response to a query by Commissioner Latvala, Mr. Burton explained that, if consensus is reached, staff will finalize the terms of the RFN, conduct another legal review, and then release the RFN in June; whereupon, Chair Eggers confirmed that there is consensus to release the RFN.\par
\par
\ul News article regarding permits to construct a pier in St. Pete Beach\par
\par
\ulnone Mr. Burton indicated that a news article was recently published which claimed that construction of a pier in St. Pete Beach was awaiting County permits; whereupon, he clarified that staff has not received an application for such permits.\cf1\f1\fs22\par

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\f0\fs24 Deviating from the order of the agenda, Chair Eggers indicated that Item No. 35 regarding the new campus design options will be presented at this time; whereupon, Mr. Burton indicated that the members are not obligated to make a decision pertaining to the design options today; and that staff is requesting input related to the project.\par
\par
Assistant County Administrator Blaine Williams introduced Kristine Bishop Johnson and Jonathan Rae from Hellmuth, Obata, and Kassabaum, Inc. (HOK); whereupon, Ms. Johnson indicated that she and Mr. Rae will provide overviews of four exterior concept designs and solicit feedback from the members; and that all four of the concept designs utilize the same palette of materials and are based on massing and siting specifications that have been approved for the location.\par
\par
Referring to a PowerPoint presentation, Mr. Rae highlighted key considerations for all four of the concept designs, including sun path and shading, public fa\'e7ades, and clear wayfinding toward and within the buildings; whereupon, in response to a query by Chair Eggers, Mr. Williams, with input from Ms. Johnson and Mr. Rae, clarified that, as part of the governance process, staff consulted with the Executive Committee and Appointing Authorities and received initial feedback regarding the design concepts; and that, since then, the exterior concepts initially distributed to the members were modified.\par
\par
During discussion regarding the design concepts, and in response to queries by Commissioner Latvala, Mr. Williams noted that while cost estimates for each design are not yet available, all four concepts utilize similar construction materials; and that each concept is anticipated to remain within budget; whereupon, in response to comments by Commissioner Scherer regarding incorporation of neoclassical design elements, Mr. Burton indicated that such features could result in significant additional costs. Ms. Johnson also explained that, due to differences in massing and proportionality, designing the campus in a classical architectural style would require substantial modifications to form, composition, aesthetic, and functionality.\par
\par
Thereupon, Mr. Rae and Ms. Johnson described the following building design concepts for the new government campus and individually highlighted their notable features:\par
\par
\ul Projected Colonnade\par
\par
\pard\fi-360\li360\ulnone\f1\'b7\tab\f0 Projected colonnade facing Ulmerton Road\par
\f1\'b7\tab\f0 Prominent judicial facade\par
\f1\'b7\tab\f0 Unique structural systems for judicial and administrative buildings\par
\pard\par
\ul Recessed Colonnade\ulnone\par
\par
\pard\fi-360\li360\f1\'b7\tab\f0 Recessed colonnade integrated into fa\'e7ade\par
\f1\'b7\tab\f0 Similar fa\'e7ade design across judicial and administrative buildings\par
\pard\ul\par
Picture Frame\ulnone\par
\par
\pard\fi-360\li360\f1\'b7\tab\f0 Shared design language\par
\f1\'b7\tab\f0 Projected frame element providing sun shading and energy reduction\par
\f1\'b7\tab\f0 Repeating fa\'e7ade elements\par
\pard\par
\ul Expressive Screen\ulnone\par
\par
\pard\fi-360\li360\f1\'b7\tab\f0 Contemporary colonnade design with metal screening system\par
\f1\'b7\tab\f0 Prominent judicial fa\'e7ade\par
\f1\'b7\tab\f0 Shared but distinct design languages\par
\pard\par
During the presentation, Mr. Rae and Ms. Johnson, with input from Messrs. Burton and Williams, responded to comments, queries, and concerns by the members regarding various aspects of the designs and discussed various topics, including the following:\par
\par
\pard\fi-360\li360\f1\'b7\tab\f0 Corner atrium function and size\par
\f1\'b7\tab\f0 Courtyard space\par
\f1\'b7\tab\f0 Parking area security and screening\par
\f1\'b7\tab\f0 Buildings\rquote expected service life based on construction materials\par
\f1\'b7\tab\f0 Energy efficiency considerations\par
\f1\'b7\tab\f0 Potential to host restaurants or food trucks on-site\par
\f1\'b7\tab\f0 Entryway design studies\par
\f1\'b7\tab\f0 Landscape concepts and integration into the Pinellas County Trail\par
\pard\par
Responding to comments and queries by Chair Eggers, Mr. Rae highlighted landscaping, the central courtyard, and sun shading as opportunities to enhance the architectural design of the campus buildings; whereupon, Ms. Johnson discussed potential enhancements for the exterior fa\'e7ade of the buildings and indicated that the design concepts present an opportunity to create welcoming public spaces and to reinforce themes of permanence, trust, and fairness in County government and the judicial system.\par
\par
The members provided additional feedback regarding the design concepts, including concerns regarding similarities with the current County campus and adherence to budget; whereupon, Mr. Williams explained that\f2\fs22 \f0\fs24 the reduced square footage of the new campus will be offset, in part, through design features intended to maximize access to natural light within workspaces.\par
\par
Thereupon, Mr. Burton acknowledged the members\rquote desire to view more contextualized campus designs and related that the presented concepts are early renditions; that staff continues to work with departments and Constitutional Officers regarding space programming; and that the concepts can be refined and presented at a future meeting.\cf1\f3\fs22\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\ul\f0\fs24 Upcoming Tax Equity and Fiscal Responsibility Act Hearing\par
\par
\ulnone Mr. Burton provided information regarding an upcoming Tax Equity and Fiscal Responsibility Act hearing for a request by Saint Paul\rquote s School, noting that the hearing will be held at the July 21 Board of County Commission meeting.\par
\par
\ul CDBG-DR Update\par
\par
\ulnone Policy recommendations with regard to the CDBG-DR program approved, with the exception of those related to reimbursement structure types, reimbursement award thresholds, and MHU relocation cases, which will be brought back to the Board for approval.\par
\b\par
\b0 Referring to a PowerPoint presentation, Disaster Recovery Program Manager Erica Henry provided an update regarding implementation of the Community Development Block Grant-Disaster Recovery (CDBG-DR) Program, including application volume, outreach efforts, and approved awards; whereupon, responding to a query by Chair Eggers, Ms. Henry explained that while application volume has slowed since immediately following the Program\rquote s launch, staff continues to conduct outreach efforts throughout the County to encourage participation.\par
\par
Ms. Henry compared the County's progress with that of other first-time CDBG-DR grantees and noted that Pinellas County continues to lead in program implementation. She also reviewed the geographic distribution of approved awards and outlined factors impacting applicant eligibility; whereupon, in response to additional queries by Chair Eggers, Ms. Henry explained that applicant eligibility may be affected by various factors, including geographic location, whether the property is a primary residence, applicant responsiveness, and voluntary withdrawal from the program; and that staff continues to identify service gaps and potential policy modifications to expand eligibility while maintaining compliance with United States Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) requirements.\par
\par
In response to queries by Chair Eggers and Commissioner Scott, Ms. Henry, with input from Horne Director Ryan Flanery, discussed factors affecting applicant eligibility, documentation requirements, applicant responsiveness, and ongoing efforts to streamline the application process while maintaining compliance with HUD requirements. Mr. Burton also noted that the County's contract with Horne incentivizes approval of eligible applications while ensuring compliance with applicable requirements.\par
\par
Responding to comments and queries by Chair Eggers, Building and Development Review Services (BDRS) Director Kevin McAndrew indicated that outreach efforts, including recent mailings, have resulted in an increased number of after-the-fact permit applications. He also noted that BDRS has partnered with the recovery team to communicate that obtaining an after-the-fact permit may allow eligible homeowners to qualify for reimbursement assistance.\par
\par
Ms. Henry then reviewed program accomplishments and discussed proposed policy recommendations intended to expand applicant eligibility and expedite assistance to eligible applicants. In response to a comment by Chair Eggers, Mr. Burton clarified incorporation of the proposed policy recommendations would not require approval by HUD; whereupon, in response to comments and queries by the members, Ms. Henry, with input from Mr. Flanery, provided additional information regarding the proposed policy recommendations, including those related to homeowner insurance requirements, homebuyer assistance awards, minimum property standards, and relocation assistance for certain mobile home owners.\par
\par
Assistant County Administrator Matthew Spoor explained that two of the proposed policy recommendations would require an Action Plan update and subsequent Board approval while the remaining recommendations may be incorporated without further action; whereupon, Ms. Henry clarified that an additional recommendation, establishing a relocation pathway for certain mobile home owners under the Homeowner Rehabilitation & Reconstruction Program, would also require an Action Plan update.\par
\par
Responding to comments and queries by Chair Eggers and Commissioner Scott, Ms. Henry provided additional information regarding the proposed policy recommendations; whereupon, Mr. Spoor indicated that the three recommendations requiring Action Plan amendments will be brought back for the Board\rquote s approval; and that the remaining recommendations can be approved separately. Ms. Henry then identified the three recommendations requiring an Action Plan update as expanding reimbursement eligibility to multifamily structure types, increasing the maximum reimbursement award for mobile home units, and establishing a relocation pathway for certain mobile home owners under the Homeowner Rehabilitation Program.\kerning2\par
}

{\rtf1\ansi\ansicpg1252\deff0\deflang1033{\fonttbl{\f0\fswiss\fprq2\fcharset0 Arial;}{\f1\fswiss\fprq2\fcharset0 Calibri;}}
\viewkind4\uc1\pard\ul\f0\fs24 Towing Update\par
\par
\ulnone Resolution No. 26-46 adopted, amending towing rates to reflect\f1\fs22 \f0\fs24 a base tow rate of $175.00, a mileage rate of $60.00, and a storage rate of $35.00.\par
\ul\par
\ulnone Referring to a PowerPoint presentation, Human Services Planning and Contract Services Division Director Tim Burns reviewed the history of the County's towing ordinance and rate adjustments, discussed implementation of a $250.00 State-level administrative lien release fee, and compared Pinellas County's current towing rates with those of neighboring counties. He also reviewed recommendations received from tow operators, including proposed adjustments to existing rates and additional fees not currently included in the ordinance.\par
\par
Responding to comments and queries by Chair Eggers and Commissioner Scott, Mr. Burns discussed implementation of the State administrative lien release fee, related consumer complaints, and ongoing litigation regarding Hillsborough County ordinance language restricting assessment of the fee during the first 48 hours following a tow. He also explained that staff is evaluating whether similar language could be incorporated into the County's ordinance.\par
\par
Mr. Burns then reviewed staff's proposed ordinance revisions, including implementation of a 48-hour waiting period before lien-related fees may be assessed, annual Consumer Price Index (CPI)-based adjustments to towing rates, an emergency fuel surcharge, an after-hours gate fee, and various ordinance clarifications. He also reviewed recommended adjustments to towing rates, which are intended to maintain competitive rates while balancing impacts to consumers.\par
\par
In response to additional comments and queries by the members, Mr. Burns, with input from Mr. Burton, provided additional information regarding various topics, including the proposed rate adjustments, the potential impact of the pending litigation associated with the Hillsborough County ordinance language, complaint trends, and the effect of the proposed recommendations on consumers and towing operators.\par
\par
Mr. Burns also reviewed consumer complaint statistics related to towing services and compared examples of consumer costs under the current ordinance, the towing industry's recommendations, and staff's proposed recommendations. Responding to a query by Commissioner Nowicki, he indicated that many complaints received from residents involved lawful tows and did not result in enforcement action; and that staff can provide additional information to the members regarding citations and warnings issued to towing operators over the last several years.\par
\par
Upon the Chair\rquote s call for public comment, Justin Heller, St. Petersburg, appeared and expressed support for updating the County's towing rates; whereupon, in response to queries by Commissioner Peters, Mr. Heller discussed increased operating costs experienced by towing operators, including expenses associated with insurance, equipment, and towing electric vehicles. Responding to queries by Chair Eggers, Mr. Heller also provided information regarding the potential cost of supplemental towing signage and the role of towing services in assisting property owners.\par
\par
Commissioner Scherer expressed concern that approval of the proposed towing rate increases could effectively result in a doubling of fees if the pending Hillsborough County ordinance litigation upholds the State administrative lien release fee and questioned whether the rate increases could automatically revert; whereupon, Attorney White explained that she would recommend against that since it would be preferable for the Board to consider any future rate adjustments through subsequent Board action since the court's ruling may not provide a sufficiently clear basis for automatically triggering such a change.\par
\par
Following lengthy discussion pertaining to the proposed towing rate adjustments and additional ordinance revisions, Commissioner Scott also expressed concern regarding implementation of the proposed towing rate adjustments prior to resolution of the pending litigation involving the State administrative lien release fee; whereupon, in response to comments by Chair Eggers, Attorney White indicated that adjustments to the existing base tow, mileage, and storage rates may be approved by the resolution included in the agenda packet; and that implementation of the remaining proposed ordinance revisions would require advertisement and consideration at a future public hearing.\kerning2\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\f0\fs24 Ordinance No. 26-21 adopted, approving amendments to the County Towing Ordinance which relate to an emergency fuel surcharge fee, Consumer Price Index (CPI) base towing rate fee increases, an electric vehicle fee, implementation of signage, and an update to statutory references related to towing. No correspondence has been received.\par
\par
Mr. Burton explained that, at the Board\rquote s request, the proposed ordinance was advertised to allow consideration of a fuel surcharge; that towing operators requested that the County review additional fees, for which staff has developed recommendations; and that staff\rquote s recommendations may vary based upon the outcome of pending litigation concerning the $250.00 administrative lien release fee; whereupon, he related that the Board may discuss the amendment at today\rquote s meeting or postpone the item until the litigation is resolved.\par
\par
Commissioner Scott expressed concern regarding the cumulative impact of the proposed fees on consumers and indicated that he would prefer to defer consideration of the ordinance until the pending litigation is resolved, noting that staff's recommendations may change depending upon the outcome; whereupon, Commissioner Scherer distributed proposed ordinance revisions and photographs illustrating conditions at a local towing facility and provided brief comments regarding additional consumer protection measures, customer service standards, and accessibility for consideration following resolution of the pending litigation.\par
\par
In response to comments and queries by Commissioner Peters, Mr. Burton provided clarifying information regarding the scope of the proposed ordinance, application of the $250.00 lien release fee, and the Board's ability to consider any of the ordinance's proposed amendments during today\rquote s meeting; whereupon, responding to a query by Chair Eggers, Human Services Planning and Contract Services Division Director Tim Burns explained that towing electric vehicles may require additional equipment and involve storage considerations; that staff proposed an electric vehicle fee of $35.00 per 15 minutes, not to exceed $70.00; and that the fee could be monitored and adjusted in the future through a resolution.\par
\par
Mr. Burton identified proposed ordinance amendments related to a late-night gate fee, a new emergency fuel surcharge fee, annual CPI base towing rate fee increases, an electric vehicle fee, implementation of new signage, and consumer outreach; whereupon, Commissioner Peters made a motion to adopt those amendments. Attorney White then advised that the specific sections mentioned in Commissioner Peters\rquote motion must be identified within the ordinance; and that the public hearing must be conducted.\par
\par
Additional discussion ensued regarding the proposed amendments wherein Commissioner Flowers seconded the motion; whereupon, in response to a query by Commissioner Flowers, Attorney White clarified that the Board can take a vote following public comment.\par
\par
Upon the Chair\rquote s call for public comment, the following individuals appeared and provided brief comments:\par
\par
Jason Goldstein, St. Petersburg (spoke on behalf of others in attendance)\par
Justin Heller, St. Petersburg\par
\par
Commissioner Latvala provided brief comments regarding the proposed late-night gate fee and expressed concern regarding its potential impact on consumers. Commissioner Peters then amended her motion to remove the late-night gate fee and retain the emergency fuel surcharge fee, CPI base towing rate fee increases, electric vehicle fee, and implementation of signage; whereupon, Commissioner Flowers seconded the amended motion.\par
\b\par
\b0 Attorney White then clarified that the proposed late-night gate fee would establish a maximum fee for after-hours access to a vehicle; and that, if the fee is not adopted, the current ordinance would continue to permit towing operators to charge an unrestricted fee for such access.\par
\par
In response to comments and queries by Commissioner Peters, Mr. Heller, with input by Rowan Cordner-James, provided information regarding application of the $250.00 administrative lien release fee; whereupon, brief discussion ensued wherein Chair Eggers expressed concern regarding moving forward with multiple ordinance amendments prior to resolution of the pending litigation and indicated that he would only support the proposed emergency fuel surcharge fee, electric vehicle fee, and implementation of signage.\par
\par
Attorney White provided additional clarification regarding the proposed late-night gate fee, including that, if no amendment is adopted, the current ordinance would continue to permit an unrestricted fee; whereupon, she identified the specific sections within the proposed ordinance that correspond to the proposed amendments and outlined the Board's options regarding the fee.\par
\par
Discussion ensued regarding after-hours access to vehicles and removal of the fee from Commissioner Peters\rquote amended motion. During discussion, Assistant County Administrator Matthew Spoor, with input from Mr. Heller, provided clarifying comments regarding the applicable ordinance sections and State requirements governing after-hours vehicle access.\par
\par
Attorney White again reviewed the ordinance sections corresponding to the motion, including implementation of new signage, the emergency fuel surcharge fee, CPI base towing rate fee increases, and the electrical vehicle surcharge; whereupon, she also indicated that staff is recommending that the Board retain a proposed update to statutory references related to towing.\par
\cf1\f1\fs22\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\f0\fs24 Referring to a PowerPoint presentation, Mr. Burton provided an overview of the proposed Fiscal Year 2027 Budget and Capital Plan, indicating that the structurally balanced proposal focuses on essential services, fiscal discipline, and future readiness; that the total proposed budget is approximately $5.137 billion, including a $1.125-billion General Fund and a $1.094-billion Capital Budget; that the General Fund has grown by 1.2% from the Fiscal Year 2026 adopted level; and that the proposal includes a reduction of 53.8 positions across all funds.\par
\par
Mr. Burton discussed challenges encountered during development of the proposed budget, including a General Fund deficit that increased from approximately $18 million to more than $30 million, unfunded mandates, reduced sales tax revenue, inflationary pressures, and rising healthcare costs. Referring to various State-mandated and external costs, he also provided information regarding Medicaid and juvenile justice payments, Florida Retirement System (FRS) costs, cybersecurity requirements, and School Board property tax collection costs; whereupon, in response to comments and queries by the members, Mr. Burton provided clarifying details regarding the amounts and requirements associated with the unfunded mandates and external costs.\par
\par
Mr. Burton then indicated that the proposed Countywide General Fund millage rate of 4.54 mills remains unchanged from Fiscal Year 2026 following four reductions during the previous five years; that the dedicated transportation infrastructure millages would likewise remain unchanged; and that General Fund reserves total approximately $169 million. He also noted that a portion of the reserves is intended to prepare for a future bond payment associated with the proposed new County campus; whereupon, in response to queries by Commissioners Peters and Scott, Mr. Burton provided information regarding the duration and continued evaluation of the transportation infrastructure millages and the progress made in addressing deficient roads, bridges, drainage systems, and other infrastructure.\par
\par
Referring to measures utilized to balance the proposed budget, Mr. Burton indicated that departments reporting to the Board reduced their General Fund budgets by approximately $16.2 million and 34.8 positions;\f1\fs22 \f0\fs24 that the Sheriff\rquote s Office reduced its request by approximately $7.3 million and 10 positions;\f1\fs22 \f0\fs24 and that additional reductions were made by the Clerk of the Circuit Court and Comptroller and Human Resources; whereupon, responding to a query by Commissioner Nowicki, he noted that reductions include both filled and vacant positions.\par
\par
Mr. Burton then reviewed the following additional proposed budget adjustments:\par
\par
\pard\fi-360\li360\f2\'b7\tab\f0 Shifting Care About Me funding to opioid abatement settlement funds\par
\f2\'b7\tab\f0 Reducing social action funding from approximately $1.7 million to $667,000.00 by maintaining funding for existing programs and eliminating funding for new programs\par
\f2\'b7\tab\f0 Shifting General Fund support for certain sexual assault survivor services to hospitals\par
\f2\'b7\tab\f0 Returning responsibility for Weedon Island Preserve and Shell Key to the State\par
\f2\'b7\tab\f0 Discontinuing County park lifeguard services\par
\pard\par
Discussion ensued regarding the proposed return of responsibility for Weedon Island Preserve and Shell Key to the State. Commissioner Flowers expressed support for retaining funding and requested that staff and the County\rquote s lobbyists pursue discussions with the Legislative Delegation regarding potential State funding for the County to continue maintaining the preserves. Chair Eggers and Commissioners Scott and Peters expressed support for preserving the properties and discussed opportunities to obtain assistance from the State, including the possibility of continuing County funding while discussions with the State take place; whereupon, Mr. Burton indicated that staff would develop options for further consideration at the upcoming work session.\par
\par
Thereupon, additional discussion ensued regarding the proposed reductions to social action funding and discontinuation of the County park lifeguard program, including the services supported by social action funding, whether such funding constitutes a core County responsibility, and the potential effects of eliminating funding for existing programs.\par
\par
Mr. Burton then reviewed the following additional proposed budget adjustments:\par
\par
\pard\fi-360\li360\f2\'b7\tab\f0 Eliminating $220,000.00 in Municipal Services Taxing Unit (MSTU) grant funding\par
\f2\'b7\tab\f0 Reducing County Administration and internal services by approximately $727,000.00 and nine positions\par
\f2\'b7\tab\f0 Strengthening requirements for employee use of GLP-1 medications\par
\f2\'b7\tab\f0 Implementing 3% budget reduction scenarios in nearly all departments reporting to the Board\par
\pard\par
Commissioner Peters and Chair Eggers expressed concern regarding the proposed elimination of MSTU grant funding and the potential impact on community projects in unincorporated areas; whereupon, Mr. Burton discussed proposed revenue adjustments, including increasing parking fees at County parks from $6.00 per day to $3.50 per hour and increasing boat ramp parking and annual pass fees. He also discussed the need to reassess core County responsibilities, consider whether other entities should bear a greater share of certain costs, evaluate measurable results and financial sustainability of services, and continue budget preparation studies.\par
\par
Referencing the Capital Plan, Mr. Burton indicated that transportation funding would continue for roads, bridges, drainage, and sidewalks; that capital investments would focus on asset management and targeted improvements; and that beach nourishment and enterprise fund projects would continue. He also related that the proposed budget includes a 3% employee salary increase, continued implementation of the Workday enterprise resource planning system, and continued planning for the new County campus.\par
\par
Mr. Burton then reviewed the remaining budget schedule, noting that Truth in Millage (TRIM) notices will be distributed on August 17; that budget work sessions will be held on August 20 and September 3; that the first public hearing will take place on September 10; and that budget adoption is scheduled for September 24.\par
\par
In response to queries by Commissioner Scott, Office of Management and Budget Director Chris Rose indicated that staff would provide additional information regarding the portion of General Fund growth attributable to new growth. Mr. Burton then provided information regarding approximately $6 million proposed for reserves and the potential use of those funds for future new campus bond costs, noting that General Fund reserves would remain at approximately two months of revenues.\par
\par
Commissioner Peters requested further consideration of existing Community Redevelopment Areas (CRAs), including the potential renegotiation of agreements or boundaries; whereupon, Mr. Burton indicated that the agreements would need to be reviewed individually with legal counsel.\par
\par
Discussion ensued regarding various topics, including the potential for additional budget reductions to achieve a full millage rollback, the effect of unfunded mandates on the County budget, and comparison of proposed expenditures to prior-year actual expenditures; whereupon, Chair Eggers suggested that staff further consider the potential for a full rollback prior to the August 20 work session.\cf1\f3\fs22\par
}

\pard\par
In response to comments by Chair Eggers regarding potential County action related to data centers, Attorney White indicated that the County Code does not currently permit data centers as a primary use; whereupon, she expressed concern that adopting a moratorium on a use that is already prohibited could create the impression that such use is otherwise allowed. Attorney White then indicated that a resolution would allow the Board to reaffirm the current prohibition of data centers and express its intent to maintain the prohibition; that future review of applicable Code definitions may be appropriate to distinguish between different types of data centers; and that a resolution could be adopted more quickly than an ordinance or moratorium.\par
\par
Following brief supportive comments by Commissioner Scott regarding the proposed resolution and its potential to address public concern, and in response to comments and a query by Commissioner Flowers regarding moratoria adopted by other local governments, Attorney White explained that the applicability and risk associated with adopting a moratorium may vary based on the provisions of each jurisdiction\rquote s code.\par
\par
Responding to comments and queries by Commissioner Peters regarding efforts by Forward Pinellas, Attorney White clarified that while Forward Pinellas may establish a countywide planning framework, restrictions regarding data centers would need to be included in the land development codes of individual local governments. Mr. Burton also noted that recent concern regarding data centers arose from inquiries involving potential sites in the unincorporated area and Pinellas Park rather than formal applications; whereupon, Chair Eggers confirmed the Board\rquote s willingness for staff and the County Attorney\rquote s Office to further review the matter and bring forward a resolution.\par
\par
Chair Eggers then provided brief comments regarding the use of Flock cameras, noting that while the technology has assisted law enforcement in solving cases, additional safeguards may be warranted to address improper or unauthorized use of the information collected; whereupon, Commissioner Scott briefly discussed public concerns surrounding the technology, including questions about its use, access to data, and data retention.\par
}

\viewkind4\uc1\pard\f0\fs24 A public hearing was held regarding the proposed Fiscal Year 2027 tentative millage rates and budgets for Pinellas County; resolutions adopted approving tentative millage rates (No. 26-70) and budgets (No. 26-71), as amended, for the Pinellas County General Fund and Health Department Fund; and resolutions adopted approving tentative millage rates (No. 26-72) and budgets (No. 26-73), as amended, for the Pinellas County Dependent Special Districts and Municipal Service Taxing Units.\par
\par
At the request of Chair Eggers, Ms. Revie reported that seven emails in opposition, regarding the tentative millages and tentative budgets, have been received by the Clerk\rquote s Office; and that the Office of Management and Budget also received 11 phone calls.\par
\par
Following a review of the sequence of events for the evening\rquote s proceedings, Chair Eggers related that Mr. Burton will provide an overview of the proposed budget, including changes that have been made following the August 11 Board of County Commission (BCC) meeting; that public comment will be accepted regarding the BCC Countywide levy for the Pinellas County General Fund and Health Department fund and the levies for Dependent Special Districts and Unincorporated Area Municipal Services Taxing Units (MSTUs); and that the resolutions for the Fiscal Year 2027 tentative millage rates and tentative budgets will be the basis for the final budget public hearing on September 24.\par
\par
Chair Eggers indicated that representatives from the Property Appraiser\rquote s Office (PAO) are available to assist anyone who has questions or concerns regarding their property\rquote s assessed value, exemptions, or classifications or information that appears on the Truth in Mileage (TRIM) notice; and that the PAO may also be contacted via phone and email.\par
\par
Chair Eggers related that, although Florida Statutes provide that a taxing authority may adopt tax levies and budgets of all its Dependent Special Taxing Districts and MSTUs by a single unanimous vote, members of the general public may request that the Board discuss and adopt any of the items separately. In response to his call for citizen participation, no one requested that an item be separately reviewed.\par
\par
Thereupon, Chair Eggers opened the first public hearing on the tentative millage rates and budgets for Fiscal Year 2027.\par
\par
Ms. Revie reported that this public hearing is being held in accordance with Chapters 129 and 200 of Florida Statutes; and that the meeting has been duly noticed by the Property Appraiser\rquote s mailing of the TRIM notice.\par
\par
Chair Eggers announced that, as taxing authority for the BCC Countywide, the Dependent Special Districts, and the MSTUs, the Board will now proceed with the public hearing.\par
\par
Mr. Burton indicated that the percentage increase in the millage rates for all budgets over the rolled-back rate, based on the maximum rates on the TRIM notice and subsequent decreases to the rates, to fund the Fiscal Year 2027 tentative budget is a 0.16% decrease over the aggregate rolled-back rate of 6.1284; whereupon, he noted that the increases in the millage over the rolled-back rate are primarily due to the following:\par
\par
\pard\fi-360\li360\f1\'b7\tab\f0 In the General Fund, including the Unincorporated Area MSTU and the Emergency Medical Services Authority, revenue increases are required to support personnel and operating expenditure levels that are driven by inflationary factors and Board priorities. With regard to the Pinellas Planning Council, sufficient revenues will exist within a millage that is equal to the rolled-back rate to support personnel and operating expenditure levels, as per the request of Forward Pinellas.\par
\par
\f1\'b7\tab\f0 In the Public Library Services District MSTU, the Palm Harbor Community Services MSTU, East Lake Library Services MSTU, East Lake Recreation Services MSTU, Greater Seminole Recreation Area MSTU, and 11 Special Fire Protection Districts, revenue increases are needed to support increased expenditures by the agencies providing services for those districts.\line\par
\f1\'b7\tab\f0 In the Feather Sound Community Services MSTU and one of the Special Fire Protection Districts, the Clearwater Fire District, sufficient revenues will exist within a decreased millage to support personnel and operating expenditure levels and Board priorities.\par
\pard\par
Thereupon, Mr. Burton reviewed a schedule of changes to the proposed budget, which he indicated is outlined in a memorandum distributed to the Board. He indicated that modifications include changes discussed at BCC meetings or work sessions and technical adjustments related to the accounting presentation, updated information, corrections, and other minor changes.\par
\par
Referring to the memorandum, Office of Management and Budget Director Chris Rose reviewed the following changes to the proposed budget, which were discussed at the August 20 and September 3 work sessions:\par
\par
\ul Changes - August 20 work session\ulnone\par
\par
\pard\fi-360\li360\f1\'b7\tab\f0 Restoration of funds for Weedon Island and Shell Key in the amount of $555,000.00 between the Parks Department and the Construction and Property Management Department\par
\pard\li360\par
\pard\fi-360\li360\f1\'b7\tab\f0 Capacity to be built for future bond payments for the new administrative campus\par
\pard\par
\pard\fi-360\li360\f1\'b7\tab\f0 Partial restoration of funding for the Unincorporated Area MSTU program in the amount of $125,000.00 from reserves\par
\pard\par
\pard\fi-360\li360\f1\'b7\tab\f0 Change in parking fees at Fort De Soto, Sand Key, and Fred Howard parks from $6.00 per day to $3.50 per hour, capped at $12.00 per day\par
\pard\par
\pard\fi-360\li360\f1\'b7\tab\f0 Transfer of one-time reserves funding in the amount of $85,000.00 to the Human Services Department to fund the first three months of services for sexual assault survivors as hospitals prepare to provide such services\par
\pard\par
\ul Changes - September 3 work session\ulnone\par
\par
\pard\fi-360\li360\f1\'b7\tab\f0 Changes in Public Works allocations and subsequent decrease in General Fund expenditures by $500,000.00\par
\pard\li360\par
\pard\fi-360\li360\f1\'b7\tab\f0 Medicaid payment from the State reduced and $975,000.00 lower than budgeted\par
\pard\par
\pard\fi-360\li360\f1\'b7\tab\f0 Closure of the Tarpon Springs Health Center and subsequent reduction of Human Services General Fund expenditures by $400,000.00\par
\pard\par
\pard\fi-360\li360\f1\'b7\tab\f0 Tax Collector excess fees revenue increase of $584,000.00\par
\pard\par
\pard\fi-360\li360\f1\'b7\tab\f0 Parking revenue increase of $285,000.00\par
\pard\par
\pard\fi-360\li360\f1\'b7\tab\f0 Water and Navigation permit fee revenue increase over three years of $283,000.00\par
\pard\par
\pard\fi-360\li360\f1\'b7\tab\f0 Removal of the General Government personnel contingency and subsequent reduction of $300,000.00\par
\pard\par
\pard\fi-360\li360\f1\'b7\tab\f0 Reduction of funds for organizational and efficiency studies in General Government by $500,000.00\par
\pard\par
\pard\fi-360\li360\f1\'b7\tab\f0 Reduction of the third dedicated millage in half, reducing funding by $1,532,000.00 and lowering associated service levels in Public Works\par
\pard\par
Mr. Rose indicated that these changes will allow the millage rate to go down by 51.4% of the State-defined rolled back rate; whereupon, he also reviewed the following non-General Fund changes:\par
\par
\pard\fi-360\li360\f1\'b7\tab\f0 Reduction of funding for the Seminole Fire District by $41,000.00 due to anticipated lower capital spending in Fiscal Year 2027, with a corresponding reduction in the proposed millage rate that would change the vote requirement for approval at the second public budget hearing from unanimous to five of seven votes\par
\pard\li360\par
\pard\fi-360\li360\f1\'b7\tab\f0 Changes with St. Pete-Clearwater Airport (PIE), including a new agreement with Allegiant Airlines providing revenue of $1,042,000.00, increased revenue from the Transportation Security Administration by $173,000.00, and the Sheriff\rquote s contract increasing expenditures by $152,000.00\par
\pard\par
\pard\fi-360\li360\f1\'b7\tab\f0 Increased Elite Event Funding by $367,500.00 for the Convention and Visitors Bureau\par
\pard\par
In response to a query by Commissioner Flowers, Mr. Burton indicated that two positions account for the increased expenditures associated with the Sheriff\rquote s contract with PIE.\par
\par
Chair Eggers announced that the BCC will continue the hearing as the taxing authority for the BCC Countywide, Dependent Special Districts, and MSTU levies by taking public comment from citizens wishing to be heard regarding the Fiscal Year 2027 budget. Upon the Chair\rquote s call for public comment, Shaquina Reese, St. Petersburg, appeared and expressed her concerns.\par
\par
Responding to comments and queries by Chair Eggers and Commissioner Peters, Mr. Burton confirmed that the changes outlined by Mr. Rose represent a 51.4% reduction in the rolled-back rate and briefly described a reduction in Public Works\rquote level of service as a result of reducing the amount of funding transferred to the Transportation Trust Fund; whereupon, discussion ensued, with input from Public Works Director Kelli Hammer Levy and Mr. Burton, regarding various topics, including the function of box culverts, flooding issues due to their age and poor condition following hurricanes, corrective maintenance performed on box culverts and roads, service coverage according to millage and budget fund, and imperative of up-to-date repairs.\par
\par
Commissioner Scott expressed concerns regarding social action funding as a discretionary expenditure and suggested its discontinuation in light of the upcoming budget year and to achieve an additional rollback; whereupon, in response to a query by Chair Eggers, Mr. Burton clarified that Commissioner Scott is referring to $667,000.00 in the budget for continuing social action funding programs; whereupon, additional discussion ensued regarding the role of the federal or local government in financing not-for-profit organizations dedicated to social issues.\par
\par
In response to queries by Commissioner Nowicki, Mr. Burton referred to a table in the aforementioned memorandum and indicated that approximately $4.1 million will be set aside for the bond payment for the new County campus; and that the inclusion of a group of programs along with the other suggested budget reduction options would amount to approximately $5.1 million, which would achieve a full rollback; whereupon, Commissioner Nowicki related that he is supportive of retaining social action funding if the amount set aside for the new campus can be decreased.\par
\par
Mr. Burton then provided brief comments regarding potential challenges associated with fulfilling a future bond payment should the amount set aside be reduced. He also provided clarifying information differentiating reserves and the set-aside amount for a bond payment for the new County campus, including that the minimum threshold for reserves remains unfulfilled since payment from the federal government is still pending; and that the amount going toward a bond payment is being phased into the budget; whereupon, Mr. Burton noted that, if the will of the Board is to provide the existing social action funding programs a one-year notice before funding is discontinued, the equivalent amount may be treated as a one-time payment and taken from reserves.\par
\par
Thereupon, in response to comments by Chair Eggers, Mr. Burton clarified that his suggestion would reduce the millage in an amount that is equal to the $667,000.00 in social action funding that was previously proposed for elimination and fund that same amount out of reserves; and that staff will require a recess to recalculate the change in millage.\par
\par
Responding to additional comments and queries by Commissioner Nowicki, Mr. Burton advised against lowering the percent threshold for reserves due to expected scrutiny as the County enters the bond market for the new campus. He also related that current reserves are below the minimum recommended level; that staff anticipates doing a short-term note of equal value to the downtown Clearwater property; that he recommends that the members not adjust the budget based on any bidding scenario for that property; and that internal borrowing could be conducted if necessary.\cf1\f2\fs22\par
}

minutes_note:
{\rtf1\ansi\ansicpg1252\deff0\deflang1033{\fonttbl{\f0\fswiss\fprq2\fcharset0 Arial;}}
\viewkind4\uc1\pard\tx720\ul\f0\fs24 Request to Declare a State of Local Emergency Due to Dengue Fever Outbreak\ulnone\par
\par
Resolution No. 26-76 adopted, declaring a State of Local Emergency as of 3:52 P.M. on September 24, 2026, as provided in Section 252.38(3)(b)5, Florida Statutes.\par
\par
Mr. Burton indicated that he is requesting declaration of a State of Local Emergency due to Pinellas County being under a mosquito-borne illness alert through the Florida Department of Health; and that increased dengue fever cases and West Nile virus activity have been observed; whereupon, he provided information regarding the number of cases confirmed and pending throughout the Tampa Bay region and the Mosquito Control and Vegetation Management section\rquote s mitigation and outreach efforts.\par
\par
Mr. Burton related that the Florida Department of Agriculture has submitted a request to the Governor to open up additional funding; that the County will likely spend $1 million above normal expenditures to account for chemicals, employee overtime, and assistive services from another County; that Pasco and Hillsborough Counties have recently passed declarations of a State of Local Emergency; and that Pinellas County following suit will allow for State reimbursement if funding is made available by the Governor.\par
\par
In response to a query by Commissioner Scott, Attorney White explained that the current declaration is drafted to allow for a State of Local Emergency for seven days; that State law was changed during the pandemic to prohibit Counties from establishing states of emergencies for longer than seven days; and that a specific provision is included in the declaration to permit the County Administrator to extend the declaration since the BCC does not meet weekly. She also related that a State of Local Emergency is limited to a maximum of 42 days; and that the State may take action should instances of the mosquito-borne illnesses spread beyond the Tampa Bay region.\par
\par
\pard Responding to comments and queries by Commissioners Latvala and Scherer, Mr. Burton indicated that the County has not experienced any fatalities. He also explained that while the State of Local Emergency would not affect time-sensitive contracts, it would enable the County to bypass traditional purchasing requirements; that staff does not intend to exercise this option; and that the recommendation of a State of Local Emergency is to allow the County to access any funds that the Governor may provide.\kerning2\par
}

\par
Referencing an anonymous email that he received and provided to the County Attorney\rquote s Office (CAO), Commissioner Nowicki expressed concern regarding the potential for protest from another bidder related to the scoring process utilized for the agreement, noting that the Federal Aviation Administration prohibits rating based on Disadvantaged Business Enterprise (DBE) status per an executive order issued in 2025; and that the above-referenced agreement is from 2024; whereupon, Attorney White noted that the CAO has not yet had the opportunity to look into the issue raised by Commissioner Nowicki.\par
\par
Responding to a query by Chair Eggers, St. Pete-Clearwater International Airport Director Mark Sprague indicated that staff could conduct research regarding the scoring process that was utilized prior to the next Board of County Commission (BCC) meeting; whereupon, Commissioner Flowers pointed out that Mr. Burton reviewed policy and contract language related to diversity, equity, and inclusion when the previously referenced executive order was issued.\par
\par
Responding to a query by Commissioner Scott, Attorney White indicated that a protest procedure is set forth in the Pinellas County Code; whereupon, Commissioners Latvala and Scherer expressed that they are not opposed to allowing staff time to review the process.\par
\par
Responding to queries by Chair Eggers and Commissioners Peters and Flowers, Mr. Sprague confirmed that he does not have any issues moving forward with the agreement and provided background information regarding the project, how the scoring process would be reviewed, possible project delays, and the minority status of the selected bidder; whereupon, Mr. Burton provided clarifying comments regarding the possibility of a project delay. In response to a query by Chair Eggers, he also confirmed that a separate discussion could be held at the next BCC meeting regarding whether it will be necessary to complete the scoring process again.\par
\par
Responding to a query by Chair Eggers, Mr. Burton, with input by Mr. Sprague, provided information regarding the current status of the passenger terminal improvements project; whereupon, Attorney White noted that the email referenced by Commissioner Nowicki appears to concern DBE goals; that the County has a Small Business Enterprise program; and that DBE goals would not have been utilized to award the contract under current policies.\cf1\f1\fs22\par
}

County Administrator authorized to execute advance funding agreements of up to $25,000.00 with Friends of Ridgecrest, Greater Palm Harbor Area Chamber of Commerce, and Crystal Beach Youth Center. Authority delegated to the County Administrator to approve and execute eight reimbursement funding agreements with East Lake Community Library, East Lake Recreation, FEAST, Feather Sound Community Services District, Greater Palm Harbor Branch YMCA, Palm Harbor Library, Palm Harbor Parks and Recreation, and Unincorporated Seminole Sports Association, as outlined in the Staff Report.\par
\par
Commissioner Peters discussed the historical distribution of MSTU Special Projects funds, noting that organizations in North County have consistently received funding through the program since 2016, while organizations in mid and south county, including Lealman, Seminole, and Tierra Verde, have submitted fewer requests. She expressed concerns that three projects associated with Seminole youth sports organizations were not recommended for funding due to the recent establishment of a separate MSTU for recreational services; and that, unlike established north county recreational programs, Seminole's programs have had limited time to develop their facilities and resources; whereupon, she requested that the Board consider funding two of the excluded projects using available reserve funds.\par
\par
In response to Commissioner Peters\rquote comments, Mr. Burton explained that certain Seminole youth sports organizations have been consolidated into a single organization and are therefore limited to one funding request under the program's guidelines. He noted that staff has expanded outreach efforts to increase awareness of the program among eligible organizations.\par
\par
Assistant to the County Administrator Audrey Ables then referred to a document titled \i FY26 MSTU Special Project Funding Applications and Recommendations \i0 and pointed out that the two projects referenced by Commissioner Peters are shade structure installations for Gulf Coast United Soccer and Seminole Seahawks, with requested funding of approximately $24,000.00 and $7,500.00, respectively.\line\line Commissioner Nowicki expressed support for the proposed shade structures but raised concerns regarding the exclusion of a funding request for the Pinellas County Veterans Association; whereupon, Mr. Burton explained that the project was not recommended for funding since the applicant lacked the required matching funds. Chair Eggers then indicated that he intends to meet with representatives of the organization regarding a potential future funding request.\par
\par
In response to queries by Commissioner Flowers, Ms. Ables clarified that the requested funding would cover installation of the shade structures; and that ongoing maintenance expenses would be covered by the Unincorporated Seminole Sports District.\par
\pard\sa160\sl252\slmult1\line\pard Discussion ensued regarding the proposed additional funding and its effect on the remaining program reserves; whereupon, Ms. Ables indicated that including the two projects would reduce the carry-forward reserve to approximately $20,000.00; and that the additional funding would be provided on a reimbursement basis.\cf1\f1\fs22\par
}

minutes_note:
{\rtf1\ansi\ansicpg1252\deff0\deflang1033{\fonttbl{\f0\fswiss\fprq2\fcharset0 Arial;}{\f1\froman\fprq2\fcharset2 Symbol;}{\f2\fswiss\fprq2\fcharset0 Calibri;}}
\viewkind4\uc1\pard\f0\fs24 A public hearing was held regarding the proposed Fiscal Year 2027 final millage rates and budgets for Pinellas County; resolutions adopted, approving final millage rates (No. 26-78) and budgets (No. 26-79) for the Pinellas County General Fund and Health Department Fund; resolutions adopted, approving final millage rates (No. 26-80) and budgets (No. 26-81) for the Emergency Medical Services Authority, Pinellas Planning Council, Unincorporated Area Municipal Services Taxing Unit (MSTU), Public Library Services District MSTU, Palm Harbor Community Services MSTU, Feather Sound Community Services MSTU, East Lake Library Services MSTU, East Lake Recreation Services MSTU, Greater Seminole Area Special Recreation MSTU, and the unincorporated portions of the Belleair Bluffs, Clearwater, Dunedin, Gandy, High Point, Largo, Pinellas Park, Safety Harbor, Seminole, South Pasadena, Tarpon Springs, and Tierra Verde Fire Protection Districts; and Resolution No. 26-82 adopted, approving the total final Fiscal Year 2027 County Budget.\par
\par
At the request of Chair Eggers, Ms. Revie reported that no correspondence has been received regarding the final millages and final budgets.\par
\par
Chair Eggers reviewed the sequence of events for the evening\rquote s proceedings and indicated that representatives from the Property Appraiser\rquote s Office are available to assist anyone who has questions or concerns regarding their property\rquote s assessed value, exemptions, or classifications or information that appears on the Truth in Millage (TRIM) notice; and that those attending virtually may contact the Property Appraiser\rquote s Office.\par
\par
Chair Eggers indicated that even though Florida Statutes provide that a taxing authority may adopt tax levies and budgets for all of its Dependent Special Taxing Districts and MSTUs by a single unanimous vote, members of the general public can request that the Board discuss and adopt any of those items separately; whereupon, in response to his call for citizen participation, Ms. Revie indicated that no individuals have pre-registered to speak virtually. Chair Eggers also confirmed that no one has requested a separate discussion.\par
\par
Thereupon, Chair Eggers opened the second public hearing on the final millage rates and budgets for Fiscal Year 2027.\par
\par
Ms. Revie reported that this public hearing is being held in accordance with Chapters 129 and 200 of Florida Statutes; that the meeting has been duly noticed by the \ldblquote Notice of Proposed Tax Increase\rdblquote and the \ldblquote Summary of the Proposed Budget\rdblquote legal advertisements that were published in the September 20, 2026, edition of the \i Tampa Bay Times\i0 ; and that affidavits stating proof of publication are to be received for filing.\par
\par
Chair Eggers announced that the Board of County Commissioners (BCC), as taxing authority for the BCC Countywide, the Dependent Special Districts, and the MSTUs, as listed above, will proceed with the public hearing.\par
\par
Mr. Burton indicated that the percentage increase in the millage rate for all budgets over the rolled-back rate, based on the maximum rates listed in the TRIM notice, to fund the Fiscal Year 2027 Final Budget is a 0.23% decrease over the aggregate rollback rate of 6.1284; whereupon, he noted that the primary purpose for the changes in the millage over the rolled-back rate are primarily due to the following:\par
\par
\pard\fi-360\li360\tx720\f1\'b7\tab\f0 In the General Fund, including the Unincorporated Area MSTU and in the Emergency Medical Services Authority, revenue increases over the rollback rate are required to support personnel and operating expenditure levels that are driven by inflationary factors and Board priorities. In the Pinellas Planning Council, sufficient revenues will exist within the millage that is equal to the rollback rate to support personnel and operating expenditure levels as per the request of Forward Pinellas.\par
\pard\f2\fs22\par
\pard\fi-360\li360\tx720\f1\fs24\'b7\tab\f0 In the Public Library Services District MSTU, the East Lake Recreation Services MSTU, the Greater Seminole Recreation Area MSTU, and 11 Special Fire Protection Districts, revenue increases are needed to support increased expenditure by the agencies providing services to those districts.\par
\pard\tx720\par
\pard\fi-360\li360\tx720\f1\'b7\tab\f0 In the Feather Sound Community Services MSTU and one of the Special Fire Protection Districts, the Clearwater Fire District, sufficient revenues will exist with a decreased millage to support personnel and operating expenditure levels and Board priorities.\par
\pard\tx720\par
Referring to a PowerPoint presentation, Mr. Burton reviewed the Fiscal Year 2027 tentative budget and provided information regarding changes discussed at previous BCC meetings, including a reduction of the millage from 4.5423 to 4.4989 and a reduction of property tax reliance of over $6 million, which is 57.9% of a full rollback and is achieved through a combination of spending reductions and additional revenue.\par
\par
Referring to Schedule A as displayed in the PowerPoint presentation, Office of Management and Budget Director Chris Rose read aloud each of the millage rates in accordance to State law; whereupon, he indicated that the aggregate millage rate is -0.23%; and that the advertisement published in the \i Tampa Bay Times\i0 is a Notice of Budget Hearing, not a Notice of Property Tax Increase. Mr. Rose also provided a brief summary of next steps to be taken upon the beginning of the new fiscal year on October 1.\par
\par
Chair Eggers related that he does not have any speaker cards for individuals who wish to participate in public comment; whereupon, Ms. Revie confirmed that no one has pre-registered to speak on the item. Noting that public comment is complete, Chair Eggers queried the members regarding any recommended changes to the final millage rates or the final budgets; whereupon, Commissioner Peters made a motion to adopt the 4.4989 millage rate, which was seconded by Commissioner Flowers.\par
\par
Chair Eggers indicated that the resolutions will now be considered to set the final Fiscal Year 2027 millage rates and budgets; that resolutions adopting the millages and budgets for the Dependent Special Districts and MSTUs require a unanimous vote; and that should a unanimous vote not be received, each resolution will need to be adopted separately.\par
\par
Mr. Burton indicated that since Schedule A has already been read, each resolution can now be announced separately for Board action; and that the Board will vote on the final millages first, followed by the final budget for each taxing authority; whereupon, responding to a query by Chair Eggers, Chief Assistant County Attorney Don Crowell referred to Commissioner Peters\rquote motion and advised that staff would like to adopt the General Fund and Health Department millage with one vote. In response to comments by Mr. Burton, Commissioner Peters restated that her motion is to adopt the Pinellas County General Fund millage and the County levy for the Health Department.\par
\par
\pard Resolution No. 26-78 adopted, approving the final Fiscal Year 2027 millage rates for the Pinellas County General fund and Health Department Fund.\kerning2\ul\par
}
title: Resolutions to adopt final millage rates and budgets for Fiscal Year 2027 (Second Public Budget Hearing).
